proffered was sufficiently specific to trigger an investigation, nor the 
decision whether or not to apply to the D.C. Circuit was judicially

The investigation at issue in this case targeted Theodore B. Olson, at 
relevant times the head of the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel 
during the first Reagan Administration. The Administration had claimed 
executive privilege over a subset of documents that had been subpoenaed 
by two House subcommittees with regard to their investigations of the 
EPA. After the matter had been settled—Superfund A d m i m‘ str a tor Rita 
Lavelle was indicted (and later convicted) on federal perjury charges 
i^eg’Rrding her misuse of Superfund money, and the EPA Administra tnr 
Anne M. Gorsuch resigned—the House Judiciary Committee sent a report 
to Attorney General Meese alleging that Theodore B. Olson, at the relevant 
time the assistant attorney general in charge of the Office of Legal Counsel, 
had “given false and misleading testimony” to Congress in defense of the 
Administration’s executive privilege claim. Although the report alleged 
also that two other Justice Department officials improperly withhold 
documents from Congress, the Attorney General applied for an 
independent counsel only with regard to Mr. Olson. The Special Division 
first appointed James C. McKay as independent counsel, but replaced him 
with attorney Alexia Morrison after Mr. McKay resigned, apparently to 
avoid an appearance of his law firm’s conflict of interest in the procAodings- 
The Supreme Court rendered this decision on the constitutionality of the 
Act after Mr. Olson and two other respondents moved to quash subpoenas 
issued by Ms. Morrison, As discussed earher, the Court rejected Olson’s 
Appointments Clause challenges, either that (a) Morrison was not an 
inferior officer and thus has to be appointed by the President with advice 
and consent or (b) the judicial appointment of a criminal prosecutor 
violated the separation of powers.
